outcome: No proof, partial case, or moved bound has been found for the conjecture that there are infinitely many safe and/or Sophie Germain primes; the two 2025 items the triage flagged either prove a different statement or are unreviewed preprints with no expert uptake, and the record search for these primes was suspended in 2024 with no new large examples found since.
summary: The conjecture (are there infinitely many Sophie Germain primes p, equivalently infinitely many safe primes q=2p+1?) remains open. Two items surfaced by the triage pass turn out, on reading past the abstract/title, not to bear on the stated question. (1) Takashi Agoh, 'A Note on Sophie Germain Primes', Integers 25 (2025) #A83 (math.colgate.edu/~integers/z83/z83.pdf, read in full): its Theorem 3.1 proves that T — the set of primes that are NOT Sophie Germain — is infinite. This is a genuine, published, expert-reviewed result (journal of record, referee acknowledged, proof by Andrew Granville personally communicated to the author for one part), but it settles the complement of the stated question, not the question itself: infinitude of non-Sophie-Germain primes is nearly trivial (in fact almost all primes are not Sophie Germain, as the paper's own density computation in Section 4 shows: primitive density of S is 0), and is a different statement from 'are there infinitely many Sophie Germain primes'. Under §3.1 this is a related/different problem sharing a namesake, not a case of the stated conjecture, so it does not count as progress on this bullet. (2) A preprint titled 'There Are Infinitely Many Sophie Germain Primes' (preprints.org 202510.1213, October 2025) does directly target the stated question, claiming a trigonometric-product-identity proof. However: preprints.org is an unreviewed, not-peer-reviewed platform; I could not access the full text (403 Forbidden on direct fetch) but WebSearch summaries of the abstract describe a trigonometric/cosecant-power/Bernoulli-polynomial argument with no indication of review or acceptance anywhere. The same platform hosts a structurally similar unreviewed preprint 'There Are Infinitely Many Mersenne Primes' (202510.0673) by a different author, and there is a documented precedent of a near-identically-titled claim (Czelakowski, 'There are Infinitely Many Mersenne Prime Numbers', Studia Logica) that was formally RETRACTED after an error was found in the proof (Theorem 7.2) — establishing that this exact rhetorical pattern ('there are infinitely many X primes' on a low-barrier preprint venue) has produced at least one confirmed false claim in an adjacent problem. No citation, critique, digestion, or any secondary discussion of the Sophie Germain preprint could be found on MathOverflow, arXiv, Tao's blog, or elsewhere. A related preprints.org item, 'Infinitude Conditions for Sophie Germain Primes' (202510.1306), could not be fetched (403) but its title suggests conditional criteria rather than an unconditional proof. Given zero expert engagement and the strong base-rate warning sign, I treat the 202510.1213 preprint as an unverified/undigested claim that does not meet even the 'claimed' bar's practical threshold of visibility, and more importantly does not change what a careful person would write in this bullet today (the live Wikipedia article on safe/Sophie Germain primes, fetched today, still states the conjecture as open with no cited 2024-2026 developments). Separately, the empirical record: the largest known Sophie Germain prime (2,618,163,402,417 × 2^1,290,000 − 1, found Feb 2016) and corresponding safe prime remain the records; PrimeGrid's Sophie Germain Prime Search subproject was suspended in 2024 after exhaustive search of its targeted ranges, and no larger example has been found since. Per §3.1, a record search extension would not move this existence question anyway even had one occurred. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this search: none of the sources (Agoh's paper, the two preprints.org items, the Wikipedia article, the speculative blog post 'Beyond the Parity Barrier' from August 2026) mention any AI system, language model, or computer-assisted proof technique of the AI kind (as opposed to ordinary computational sieve search for prime records, which is not AI under §6.2).
competing_reading: One could argue the Agoh result, by pinning down exactly how the complement T relates to S via the explicit set A (Theorem 2.1), constitutes indirect structural progress toward understanding S — but the paper itself explicitly proves only facts about T's infinitude and S's density being 0, and never claims or implies anything toward S's infinitude; the author's own framing treats T's infinitude as the 'almost self-evident' but technically fiddly result, with S's infinitude left conspicuously untouched. I am confident this is a related/complementary result, not a case of the stated problem, but flag the reading here since it is the same author, same year, same paper as the triage's top lead.
what_would_settle_it: Direct access to the full text of preprints.org 202510.1213 (currently blocked to automated fetching) to check whether its trigonometric identity argument is complete and whether it has since been withdrawn, corrected, or picked up by any reviewer; and continued monitoring of arXiv/Integers/journals for any successor to Agoh's note that addresses S's infinitude directly rather than T's.
